column4: The source section's dictionary branch defines olive oil as an extract and as a food condiment; this ayah itself joins a tree from Sinai that grows oil with relish for eaters, making the oil both yield and food.
The source section names olive oil as a use of the olive; here oil from a blessed olive tree nearly shines without fire, extending the food-bearing tree into the surah's distinct image of light.
The source section identifies the olive by root ز ي ت and follows its oil as provision; this ayah places olives among the crops and fruits grown by rain, locating that provision in rain-fed growth.
The source section's named word is the olive; this rain-grown inventory includes olive and pomegranate, said to be alike and unlike, adding variety within the provision of fruit.

The source section treats olives and figs as edible produce; this ayah names olives among gardens, dates, grapes, and pomegranates, then tells people to eat at harvest and give its due, tying the produce to use and distribution.

The source section moves from edible fruit to food that sustains; this ayah grows date palms and grapevines into gardens with abundant fruits for people to eat, a parallel form of food-bearing provision.

The source section's wording explicitly pairs the human and the olive through 80:24 and 80:29; this ayah itself commands a person to consider his food, turning the meal into an inquiry developed by the following crop sequence.
The source section explicitly notes its human-and-olive pairing with this ayah; 80:29 itself names olives and date palms among the crops, locating the olive in a human food sequence.

The source section's dictionary entry describes oil as provision given to a group; 80:31 names fruit and fodder, and 80:32 itself identifies the sequence as provision/enjoyment for people and livestock.
The source section treats fruit as food and one kind of sustenance; this ayah says rain produces fruits as provision for people, making that everyday yield an explicit divine provision.
The source section's named image is edible fruit as provision; here rain brings forth fruits as provision for people, directly joining the fruit image to rizq.
The source section links fruit with a secure city; Abraham's prayer in this ayah asks for both a secure town and fruits for its people, holding safety and food together in one request.

The source section pairs safe dwelling and fruit provision; Abraham's prayer places his family in a barren valley and asks that they be provided fruits so they may give thanks, making provision a requested gift where cultivation is absent.
The source section joins safety with fruit provision; this ayah asks whether the people were established in a secure sanctuary to which fruits from every kind of place are brought.
The source section links a community's food and security; this ayah itself joins being fed against hunger with being made safe from fear, and 106:2 supplies the chapter's seasonal travel setting.
The source section's dictionary gloss calls manna food God bestowed, and explicitly notes its meeting with the Tūr; this ayah names manna and quails after Israel's rescue and the promise at Tūr.
The source section identifies manna and quails as bestowed food; this ayah again names both and tells Israel to eat the good things provided, placing the gift among God's provisions.

The source section identifies manna and quails as food God gave Israel; this ayah names them with cloud shade and the instruction to eat good things provided, showing the gift in its own wilderness setting.

The source section's dictionary gloss presents manna as food God provided; following the manna in 20:80, this ayah tells Israel to eat the good things provided and warns against transgression, adding the required response to that food.

The source section explicitly labels its q-w-m root gloss as what sustains and suffices; this ayah calls wealth a qiyām for people and says to provide from it food and clothing, giving that support a concrete material form.

The source section explicitly connects the q-w-m root to a means of livelihood and explains qiyāman li-n-nās as what supports people's living and return; this ayah calls the Sacred House a qiyām for people, anchoring that gloss in its Quranic wording.
The source section says provision reaches across two worlds and joins material rizq to promised reward; this ayah itself pairs provision in heaven with what people are promised.

The source section moves from edible provision to the reward for righteous deeds; this address to messengers places eating good things and acting righteously in the same command, joining nourishment and conduct without equating food with reward.

The source section's fruit and oil are material yields and its ajr is a lasting return; this ayah makes a seed producing many ears the image for multiplied spending in God's way, joining harvest to reward.

The source section labels manna as a divine food-gift and mamnūn as the word for uninterrupted reward; this ayah uses the same root in its distinct sense of reproaching recipients after spending, then promises the spenders their reward, clarifying the root's different senses around giving.

The source section treats fruit as provision that leads to an enduring reward; this ayah compares sincere spending to a garden that yields twice its fruit after rain, using produce to make the reward-bearing act perceptible.
The source section quotes mamnūn for reward that does not run out; this ayah repeats أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ for believers who do good, directly showing the same reward wording elsewhere.
The source section quotes mamnūn for reward without end; this ayah gives the Prophet an ajr ghayr mamnūn, extending the same wording to a different addressee.
The source section quotes mamnūn for uninterrupted reward; this ayah gives believers who do good the same ajr ghayr mamnūn, pairing the phrase with faith and action as in the section.

The source section turns perishable food into an image of reward without interruption; this description of the promised garden says its food is lasting, directly setting enduring provision beside its worldly kinds.
The source section connects fruit to ajr ghayr mamnūn; this ayah describes garden fruit as neither cut off nor withheld, a specific unbroken supply of the same food the section begins with.

The source section moves from food fruit to lasting reward; this ayah describes garden dwellers repeatedly receiving fruit and recognizing what was provided before, making repeated provision part of the afterlife image.
The source section calls its fruit, oil, and manna forms of rizq and links rizq to reward; 37:42 names fruit for the people of 37:41's known provision, while this ayah supplies that provision frame.
The source section treats fruit as food and as the start of a line toward reward; following 37:41's known provision, this ayah names fruit and honor for the recipients.
The source section connects material provision to an enduring reward; 37:42 names the fruit, and 37:43 itself locates its recipients in gardens of bliss.
The source section treats fruit as a kind of provision and reward as its enduring form; this ayah says the garden's people are supplied with fruit and meat, a concrete afterlife provision.
The source section extends fruit and oil into the idea of sustained provision; this garden description includes fruits among its promised provisions, alongside rivers of several kinds.
The source section treats fruit as food and sustenance; this ayah promises fruit to the garden's people and adds that they have what they ask, making the supply part of their recompense.
The source section identifies fruit as edible provision; this ayah tells garden dwellers they have abundant fruits from which they eat, giving the afterlife counterpart.
The source section calls the continuing wage a form of provision; this ayah joins entry into the Garden for good deeds with being provided there without reckoning.
The source section says provision spans both worlds and calls the reward unending; this ayah describes the garden's people receiving provision morning and evening, a continuing afterlife supply.
The source section uses mamnūn for an unending wage; this ayah describes the blessed people's gift as not cut off, a parallel account of an unbroken return.

The source section's dictionary gloss pictures olive oil as table food and its prose also names manna as food from above; this ayah's disciples ask for a table sent down from heaven, meeting the table and heavenly-food strands in a distinct scene.

The source section joins ordinary food with provision from heaven; after the request in 5:112, this ayah says the disciples want to eat from the table and have their hearts reassured, adding their reason for asking.

The source section's table-food and bestowed-provision strands meet here: 5:113 states the disciples' wish to eat, and this ayah has Jesus ask for a heavenly table as a feast for the first and last of them and a sign.
The source section shows a town losing provision after ingratitude; following the heavenly table request in 5:114, this ayah makes disbelief after the delivered meal a boundary with punishment.

The source section recalls manna and quails as provisions in Israel's wilderness story; this ayah adds water from the rock for each tribe and tells them to eat and drink from God's provision, another concrete form of sustenance in that same story.

The source section's food image is explicitly paired with the olive in 80:24 and 80:29; 80:24 sets the food question, and 80:25 itself supplies the poured water that begins the sequence explaining its source.
After 80:25's poured water, this ayah contributes the earth being split, the stage before the crops named in 80:27–31 and the provision identified in 80:32.
After 80:26 opens the earth, this ayah names grain as the first crop in the sequence that ends with provision in 80:32, adding a direct food crop.
Following grain in 80:27, this ayah names grapes and green fodder; the source section's edible fruit and provisions image makes these another concrete crop and animal food.
After 80:29's olives and date palms, this ayah adds dense gardens to the food-growing scene that 80:32 calls provision for people and livestock.
The source section identifies fruit as food; after the gardens in 80:30, this ayah names fruit and pasture before 80:32 identifies the sequence as provision.
The source section's named olive provision appears in 16:11; this preceding ayah supplies the rainwater and trees that frame the following olive and fruit yield.
The source section treats the olive and other fruit as nourishment; this ayah points to dead earth revived and grain from it as food, connecting provision to the land's renewal.
Following the grain from dead earth in 36:33, this ayah names date palms and grapes with springs, extending the edible growth scene.
The source section describes fruit as an eaten gift; after the gardens in 36:34, this ayah names their fruit for people to eat and raises the question of gratitude for what they did not make.
The source section locates fruit and oil within provision; this ayah starts a rain scene with blessed water and gardens and harvested grain, setting up the provision named in 50:11.
After 50:9's rain and gardens, this ayah adds tall date palms with clustered fruit, a concrete food-bearing tree before the provision conclusion.
The source section names fruit and food as rizq; following the rain, grain, and date palms in 50:9–10, this ayah identifies them as provision for servants and evidence of revival.
The source section treats fruit as food and provision; this ayah names fruit and date clusters in the earth-garden scene, giving specific produce rather than an abstract blessing.
After the fruit and date clusters in 55:11, this ayah adds grain with husk and fragrant plants, expanding the scene to staple food and edible growth.

The source section's dictionary gloss says oil could be given as travel provisions; this pilgrimage instruction tells people to take provisions and then names reverent fear as the best provision, connecting carried food to the section's turn from bodily sustenance toward moral return.

The source section's dictionary branch includes oil as provisions for a group; during their journey, Moses asks his companion for their lunch after travel fatigue, a specific carried meal in a travel scene.

The source section defines figs and olives as things eaten and traces oil as food; this ayah describes dates and grapes yielding drink and good provision, broadening the tree-food image while distinguishing good provision from another use.

The source section moves from worldly food and livelihood to an unending wage; this ayah calls the Lord's provision better and more lasting than the worldly life's adornment, making the time-bound/lasting distinction explicit.

The source section turns material provision into a comparison with lasting reward; this ayah calls wealth and children worldly adornment and the remaining good deeds better in reward and hope, stating that boundary in its own terms.
The source section ends its food-and-livelihood line with reward that does not end; this ayah says worldly gifts are enjoyment and adornment while what is with God is better and more lasting.

The source section distinguishes worldly forms of sustenance from an enduring wage; this ayah calls what people receive in this life enjoyment and says what is with God is better and lasting for believers.
The source section moves from earthly food to reward without end; 87:17 says the Hereafter is better and more lasting, while this ayah supplies the contrasted preference for the nearer life.
Following 87:16's preference for the nearer life, this ayah says the Hereafter is better and more lasting, a direct boundary for the source section's move from ordinary provision to unending reward.

The source section contrasts edible worldly yield with an unending wage; this ayah compares worldly life to rain-grown plants that later yellow and crumble, making the perishing side of that contrast visible.

The source section's secure, well-provided town turns through ingratitude into hunger and fear; this ayah gives the opposite boundary, saying belief and mindfulness would open blessings from heaven and earth to town-dwellers.

The source section cites 16:112's town losing abundance through ingratitude; this ayah states the fitting response to provision—eat what God has provided and be grateful—so its own contribution is gratitude at the meal.
The source section develops fruit as provision; this ayah opens a parable with two date-and-grape gardens and crops, setting a concrete scene of abundant livelihood.
The source section's fruit image is one of harvested provision; following 18:32's two gardens, this ayah says each produced its yield and had a river, specifying their productivity.

The source section sets food and livelihood beside an enduring reward; after the productive gardens in 18:33, this ayah describes their owner boasting of abundant fruit and wealth, exposing confidence in material provision.

The source section reserves unendingness for the righteous wage; this ayah's garden owner assumes his orchard will never perish, a pointed contrast between imagined permanence of earthly fruit and the section's promised lasting return.

After 18:35's claim that the garden will not perish, this ayah denies the Hour and expects an even better return; it makes the source section's distinction between worldly abundance and the afterlife reward concrete.
The source section shows abundant provision vulnerable to reversal; this ayah warns that a garden's owner may wake to a calamity sent from heaven, directly placing crop security at risk.
Following the threatened calamity in 18:40, this ayah names the garden's water sinking away; it identifies the loss of the source that sustains fruit-bearing land.

The source section links fruit and provision with their possible loss; after 18:41's water disappears, this ayah says the garden's fruit is surrounded and its owner regrets his association, completing the reversal.

The source section's produce is food and provision; this ayah describes Sheba's two gardens and commands their people to eat their Lord's provision and give thanks, directly joining fruit, livelihood, and response.
Following 34:15's two gardens and grateful provision, this ayah says a flood changed them into bitter, sparse gardens, a direct reversal of abundant edible yield.
After the garden loss in 34:16, this ayah names ingratitude as the reason for the repayment, completing the provision-and-response pattern also developed in the source section.

The source section pairs a safe sanctuary with gathered fruits in 28:57; this next ayah recalls towns that exulted in their livelihood and were destroyed, putting a boundary around confidence in abundant provision.
The source section itself draws on this reversal: the ayah moves from a secure, content town receiving ample provision from everywhere to ingratitude, then to the garment of hunger and fear.

The source section names manna as food bestowed on Israel; in this continuation of the wilderness meal story, the people reject one food and ask for vegetables and lentils from the earth, reversing gratitude for a given provision.

The source section moves from fruit as provision to a reward that will not be cut off; this ayah asks about a date-and-grape garden with many fruits destroyed by a fiery whirlwind in its owner's old age, a precise image of vulnerable worldly yield.
